newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian markets seen set to gain on rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Italian markets seen set to gain on rate cut.

text.p: Italian financial markets, taken by surprise over the timing of a 50 basis point cut in official interest rates, are likely to rise in appreciation of the long-sought move by the Bank of Italy, analysts said.

The central bank, after dampening fervid market speculation last month that a rate cut was imminent, announced after markets closed last Friday it was easing the discount rate to 6.25 percent and the fixed term advances or Lombard rate to 7.75 percent.

"The rate cut was not totally expected after very tough comments by Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio and therefore the reaction should be quite positive," said Lorenzo Codogno, chief economist at Bank America here.

"The lira should remain quite stable. I would expect a good reaction on the BTP (government bond) market and also in the equity market," he said, adding BTP futures could gain 100 basis points from current levels.
Italian debt and stock markets have rallied almost in a straight line in the past two weeks on optimism Italy will be among the founders of a single European currency in 1999.

After forging a series of record highs, markets eventually paused last Thursday and Friday. The September BTP future on LIFFE, which peaked at a record of 134.84, ended European trade on Friday just above the 134.00 level.
The yield spread between the benchmark 10-year BTP and the 10-year German bund also narrowed into a record 111 basis points, although by Friday it was back out around 120.
The lira has crept up only gradually and is currently quoted at 976 per mark after sticking close to that level all week.
On the stock market the Mib30 blue-chip index last week reached 20,631, the peak since its creation four years ago.
Stocks are not quite at the record of 1986 when Italy's BCI index hit 908.20. The BCI, which is updated once a day, is now at 836.83 but Codogno saw it testing the record.

Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas in London, also expected markets to gain. "There'll be some more mileage in the market come Monday. This is an encouraging factor. Italy's beginning to play catch-up on rates."
Italy has trailed other Europeans in trimming official rates and while this is the fourth cut in nearly a year, analysts and industry have urged Fazio for months to lower the cost of money.
But Fazio had indicated that although data showed consumer prices at their lowest levels for nearly 30 years, he was not convinced inflation had been quashed thoroughly.
He also wanted the government to take steps to keep the budget deficit under control in order to meet a 3.0 percent deficit to gross domestic product goal needed to join the single currency.

Codogno said he expected the impact of the cut to be seen at the long end of the yield curve first, with short term rates not decreasing much initially but with the BTP-Bund spread down at 100 basis points in the course of the month.
Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets here, doubted the cut would have much impact saying the market had already factored it in with eurolira rates fully discounting the move.
"It was 100 percent discounted particularly because it's only 50 basis points rather than 75. The issue is when will we get the next cut," De Gregorio said.
He expected another easing in September when the government had presented its 1998 budget and achieved agreement with trade unions and employers over crucial pension reforms.
Mario Noera at Deutsche Bank here said markets could retrace a little initially but added: "The trend won't reverse because there's still room to ease again."
--Milan bureau +392 66129507
